name: nickle
why: A C-like desk calculator language with arbitrary precision and a real interpreter is a delightful, underused little language.

brief.what_it_is: Nickle is a programming language and prototyping environment that vaguely resembles C. It handles arbitrary precision integers, arbitrary precision rationals, and unbounded floating-point reals with specifiable precision, alongside arrays, strings, structures, tagged unions, and pointers. The homepage says it provides the functionality of UNIX bc, dc and expr in improved form, and can serve as a scripting tool or a replacement for spreadsheets in some uses. The homepage does not say what the input and output formats are beyond this.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage presents Nickle as a language-based prototyping environment for numeric work, meant to go beyond bc, dc and expr and to complement the limited numeric support of AWK and Perl.
brief.how_it_works: The homepage describes optional static type checking backed by full run-time type checking, and a simple thread model with semaphores and mutexes. It also mentions typed exceptions, first-class functions, and continuations, drawn from Modula 3, ML and Java. It does not explain the interpreter's internals on this page.
brief.install_notes: The homepage says the current version is normally in Debian unstable: run 'apt-get update' then 'apt-get install nickle'. Release builds are also offered as .deb, .rpm and .tar.gz from a release directory, and the git master is described as canonical. Nightly snapshots are built each morning when git has changed. The homepage gives no Homebrew-specific notes, and it does not describe first-run configuration.
brief.standout: Its numeric core is the selling point: exact rationals and arbitrary precision reals in a C-like language, with a dc/bc heritage. It also pairs that with an FFI that Keith Packard used for a Cairo binding (cairo-5c), and with a 2001 Usenix paper that describes the design.
brief.status: quiet: the homepage was last updated 2005/04/02, and the page shows no newer release date. Recent activity is not confirmed from this page, so treat it as unverified.
brief.caveats: The homepage is dated 2005 and may not describe the current release. It says parametric polymorphism and more ADT support are still unimplemented, and a few C features are missing or differ. It also says stale versions exist and should be avoided. No licence is named on the page beyond the 2001-2002 copyright line for Keith Packard and Bart Massey. The README was not available because the homepage is not a GitHub repository.
quotes: Nickle is a programming language based prototyping environment with powerful programming and scripting capabilities.
Nickle provides the functionality of UNIX bc, dc and expr in much-improved form.
The git master is canonical, though.
fetch_log: https://www.nickle.org/ - worked; returned the homepage text, which links to a tutorial, manual, paper, mailing list and git repository, but the page text gives no URLs for those, so I did not follow any further links.

judge.reason: Nickle’s exact rational and arbitrary-precision real arithmetic inside a C-like scripting language makes an unexpectedly deep desk calculator, though its current maintenance is unclear.

entry.title: Nickle
entry.tldr: A C-like desk calculator language with exact rationals and arbitrary precision numbers, built as a fuller replacement for bc, dc and expr.
entry.deeper_look:
Nickle is a small programming language aimed at numeric work. Its syntax looks like C, but the numbers behave differently: integers have no size limit, rationals are exact, and floating-point reals carry a precision you choose. Arrays, strings, structures, tagged unions and pointers sit alongside them.

The homepage says it was built to provide the functionality of UNIX bc, dc and expr "in much-improved form". It is meant to fill the gap between a calculator and a full language, and to cover what AWK and Perl handle poorly in numeric work. It can run scripts, or it can be used as a prototyping environment for numeric ideas.

Under the calculator surface is a real language. The homepage describes optional static type checking backed by full run-time type checking, typed exceptions, first-class functions, continuations, and a simple thread model with semaphores and mutexes. It says these ideas are drawn from Modula 3, ML and Java.

The design is described in a 2001 Usenix paper. Keith Packard also used Nickle's foreign function interface to build a Cairo binding, cairo-5c. It is an old, quiet corner of language design that is still pleasant to type into.

try_this.what_happens: Prints the interpreter's command-line options so you can see how to start it and run scripts.

entry.whats_unique: It combines exact rationals and unbounded-precision reals with a C-like syntax and a real type system, instead of bc's terse calculator dialect.
entry.caveats: The homepage was last updated in 2005 and may not match the current release; it says parametric polymorphism and fuller ADT support are still unimplemented.
